newsitem.title: UK: Lloyds leads banks lower on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Lloyds leads banks lower on profit-taking.

text.p: UK bank stocks dropped on Wednesday as some investors cashed in gains from the sector's surge of recent weeks, yet analysts and dealers said a shortage of stock in the sector could still propel it higher in the short term.
"We are saying it's too early to take profits," said the head of equity trading at one brokerage. "They will go higher."

Lloyds TSB, which set a record 584p in early trade on Tuesday, was down 16-1/2p or 2.9 percent at 558 by 1445 GMT, Barclays Plc was down 18p at 11.43 stg, National Westminster Bank Plc was down 26p at 725 and Abbey National Plc was down 6p at 845-1/2.

The gains in banking stocks have been a key issue for the UK equity market in recent sessions, helping -- along with drug and utility stocks -- drive the market sharply higher from its mid-April trough.
"If you havn't been in the banks, pharmaceuticals or utilities you haven't been making money," said another dealer.

Yet the sector's increase has largely been due to the difficultlies for investment institutions in buying shares in demutualising building societies, forcing them to up their holdings of existing banks in order to reflect the increasing size or weighting of the sector.
With the biggest demutualisation yet -- Halifax -- still to come, participants said the sector could be squeezed still higher.
"Bank shares have had a very good run and I think today's move has been a combination of profit-taking and the downward move by the market," said Kathryn Newton, banking analyst at UBS.
"In the short-term, we do expect bank stocks to be held up by the Halifax and Woolwich coming to the market and I don't think today's move is the beginning of the end."

Yet others cautioned that the recent spike did not reflect a view on the sector's underlying prospects and that the threat of increasing competition between the growing number of quoted companies could bear down on the shares.
"Short term there is a technical situation, there is an artificial stock shortage, but that is not a fundamental reason to purchase the shares," said the head equity trader at another top brokerage.
"Longer term they will all be fighting for business and margins will be under pressure...there's value elsewhere in the market."
